Chapter 13 Vibration of continuous systems: string, shaft and beam

13.6 Modes of a beam

For the string and the bar, the equation of motion has a second derivative in space, so the modes were sines. For the beam it has a fourth derivative. What shape does a beam take when it vibrates in one mode (definition 13.6), and at which frequencies? Chapter 12 gave approximations with the consistent and the lumped mass of a beam, and the values with the consistent mass lay above the true ones (errors in figure 13.100). Now we compute the true value and compare the approximations with it (section 13.6.12).

From history

Jacob Bernoulli wrote that the curvature of a bent bar at each point is proportional to the bending moment at that point. He computed the constant wrongly because of a mistaken assumption about the axis of rotation of the cross section, but the general form of the relation was correct and Euler used it later (TIMO, PDF p. 35). It is the relation \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of chapter 5. Daniel Bernoulli suggested to Euler in a letter that he should use the calculus of variations to find the shape for which \(\int \mathrm{d}s/r^2\) is a minimum, where \(r\) is the radius of curvature. Up to a constant factor this integral is the strain energy of a bent bar (TIMO, PDF p. 35). Euler worked this out in the appendix on elastic curves to his book of 1744 (TIMO, PDF pp. 37 and 39). Daniel Bernoulli was also the first to derive the differential equation of the lateral vibration of prismatic bars and used it to study particular modes of the motion, and Euler integrated it (TIMO, PDF p. 36). Bernoulli made a series of experiments on the position of the nodes, that is the points that stay at rest during the vibration, and on the pitch of the tone, and wrote to Euler that they agree with the theory (TIMO, PDF p. 36). For vibration Euler took small deflections, so that the second derivative equals the curvature, and clamped the bar vertically at one end so that gravity does not affect the motion (TIMO, PDF p. 42). A small piece of the bar moves like a pendulum, so the force toward the axis is proportional to the displacement of the piece (TIMO, PDF pp. 42-43). Euler concluded that the bar at rest would take the same curvature as during the vibration if a force proportional to the displacement acted on each piece (TIMO, PDF p. 43). The reason is that in one mode all points vibrate with a common time dependence \(\cos\omega t\), so the acceleration of each point is \(-\omega^2\) times its displacement and the force the bar must supply is proportional to the displacement. He obtained the equation of motion by differentiating the relation between curvature and moment twice, because the second derivative of the moment equals the intensity of the lateral load (TIMO, PDF p. 43). The load is here the force of the piece due to its displacement, which gives \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = \rho A\,\omega^2 w\), the equation of this section for one mode. TIMO says that Euler thus reached a conclusion that we now reach with d'Alembert's principle, and that he did not know d'Alembert's book of 1743 when he wrote the appendix (TIMO, PDF p. 43, footnote). He integrated the equation and found the frequency equation from the end conditions, for the cantilever, simply supported ends, clamped ends and both ends free, and for all these cases a formula for the frequency with a number that depends on the end conditions and on the mode (TIMO, PDF pp. 43-44). He also proposed to determine from the frequency, by experiment, the stiffness that he called the "absolute elasticity" (TIMO, PDF p. 44).

The story showed that the mode of a beam is fixed by a fourth derivative, driven by the force of the displacement itself, and that the frequency is fixed by the end conditions and the mode. So we now write the mode of the beam and compute the frequencies.

We study a straight prismatic beam of length \(L\) in the Euler-Bernoulli model (definition 5.14). The axis \(x\) lies along the beam, \(w(x, t)\) is the transverse deflection (poves) at time \(t\), and the stiffness \(EI\) and the mass per length \(\rho A\) are constant. The beam carries no load, so by theorem 13.37 (equation (13.42) with \(q = 0\))

\[\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = 0 .\]

The model has three named idealizations. The first is the Euler-Bernoulli one: cross-sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis, so there is no shear deformation, and the turning of the cross-sections is neglected. As a measure of smallness we take the radius of gyration \(r = \sqrt{I/A}\), a length that is \(11{,}5\) mm for the \(20 \times 40\) mm section (height \(40\) mm in the plane of bending), so \(r/L = 0{,}0115\) at \(L = 1\) m. Section 13.10 computes that at this slenderness the turning of the cross-sections and then shear lower the first frequency of a simply supported beam by \(0{,}066\) % and \(0{,}270\) %, and for a short beam \(L = 80\) mm (\(r/L = 0{,}144\)) by \(8{,}9\) % and \(24{,}9\) %. The model therefore holds for slender beams. The second idealization is a small slope: the equation is linear because we take \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) for the curvature of the axis in place of the exact \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}/(1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)^{3/2}\) (chapter 5) and neglect the stretching of the axis. Chapter 5 and section 13.5 allow a slope up to \(0{,}1\), at which the factor \((1 + w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)^{-3/2}\) differs from \(1\) by at most \(1{,}5\) %. Here we take the stricter bound \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}01\), at which this difference is at most \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\). We take the stricter bound because the bound \(0{,}1\) would allow a tip displacement of \(73\) mm in the first mode of the cantilever, while the steel of the beam of the introduction (\(E = 196\) GPa, yield stress \(220\) MPa) yields at the clamp already at a tip displacement of about \(16\) mm. In the first vibration of the cantilever (figure 13.87) the largest slope, when the tip is displaced by \(1\), is \(1{,}3765/L\), so the slope stays below \(0{,}01\) as long as the tip displacement does not exceed \(0{,}01\,L/1{,}3765 = 7{,}3\) mm at \(L = 1\) m. The third idealization is ideal supports: the clamping is perfectly rigid and the simple support frictionless. A real wall rotates a little, so a real end is not as stiff as a perfect clamp. We expect that a real beam therefore vibrates somewhat more slowly than we compute, but we do not prove it here.

For numbers we take the steel beam of chapters 5 and 12: section \(20 \times 40\) mm, bending in the plane of height \(40\) mm, \(L = 1\) m, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³, \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m², \(\rho A = 6{,}24\) kg/m. The computations are in SymPy, mpmath and NumPy. Figure 13.73 shows these dimensions on the section on the left and on the beam seen from the side on the right. On the left is the rectangular section with the \(20\) mm dimension for the width and the \(40\) mm dimension for the height, and the arrow \(w\) shows the direction of the deflection in the plane of the height. On the right is the side view of the beam with its length \(L\), which is in reality much longer and is shortened here.

13.6.1 End conditions

A beam end is supported in one of three ways that we know from chapter 5, and figure 13.74 shows them one under the other. The blue curve in each row is the deflection of the beam and the grey dashed line is the axis before bending. A clamp has a wall and allows neither displacement nor rotation: the curve leaves the wall on the axis and horizontally. A simple support has a support that allows no displacement but transmits no moment, so the moment there is zero: the curve starts on the axis and its slope is free. A free end has no support and transmits neither force nor moment, so the curve may leave the axis and tilt there. The conditions beside each row are written in the definition that follows. The signs are as in chapter 5: moment \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), shear force \(V = -M_{\mathrm{x}} = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\).

Definition 13.39 Clamped, simply supported and free end of a beam (vpet, prostoležeč in prost konec nosilca)

Let \(e\) be one of the ends \(0\) or \(L\) of a beam with deflection \(w(x, t)\). The end \(e\) is, as in figure 13.74,

  • clamped (vpet) if \(w(e, t) = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t) = 0\) at every time \(t\),
  • simply supported (prostoležeč) if \(w(e, t) = 0\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(e, t) = 0\) at every time \(t\),
  • free (prost) if \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(e, t) = 0\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}(e, t) = 0\) at every time \(t\).

Source: CK (13.15) to (13.17), PDF p. 411, GR (4.244), PDF p. 286. The conditions on the moment and the shear force are the natural conditions of theorem 13.37 with zero force and moment at the end.

The clamp conditions are essential (displacement and slope are prescribed). The conditions at a free end are natural, the principle gives them by itself (section 13.5). At a simple support the displacement is prescribed and the zero moment is a natural condition.

Figure 13.75 shows what one mode means. The grey dashed line is the undeformed axis of the beam, the blue curve is the deflection at three times, \(t = 0\), \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), written in the labels on the left. An example of the shape is a sine, used here only for drawing. The orange curve is the time factor \(\cos\omega t\) with the horizontal axis \(t\), and the blackwhite dots on it are three instants at which the factor has the values \(1\), \(0{,}5\) and \(-0{,}8\). At each instant the deflection is the same shape multiplied by that value, so at \(t_1\) it is half as high and at \(t_2\) it is turned downward.

For a beam, definition 13.6 means the following: the beam vibrates in the same shape \(\varphi(x)\) at all times, \(w(x, t) = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) with \(\omega > 0\), and satisfies the equation of motion and the conditions at both ends. The theorem says what must then hold for \(\varphi\).

Theorem 13.40 Eigenvalue equation of a beam (lastna enačba nosilca)

Let the beam have at each end the conditions of definition 13.39, let \(\omega > 0\) and let \(\varphi\colon [0, L] \to \mathbb R\) be a four times continuously differentiable function that is not identically zero. The pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the beam (definition 13.6, shape times time factor) if and only if

\[\varphi'''' = \beta^4\,\varphi \quad \text{on } [0, L] , \qquad \beta^4 = \frac{\rho A\,\omega^2}{EI} , \quad \beta > 0 , \tag{13.47}\]

and the end conditions hold for \(\varphi\) in place of \(w(\cdot, t)\): clamped end \(\varphi(e) = \varphi'(e) = 0\), simply supported \(\varphi(e) = \varphi''(e) = 0\), free \(\varphi''(e) = \varphi'''(e) = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the time factor \(\cos\omega t\) is a common factor of every equation and is not identically zero.

  1. By theorem 8.13, \((\cos\omega t)'' = -\omega^2\cos\omega t\), and \(\cos\omega t\) is not identically zero because \(\cos 0 = 1\) (the first dot on the curve).
  2. For \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) (blue curve times the factor) we have \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = \varphi''''\cos\omega t\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2\varphi\cos\omega t\), and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\) are \(\varphi'\), \(\varphi''\), \(\varphi'''\) times \(\cos\omega t\). The equation of motion is therefore \(\big(EI\,\varphi'''' - \rho A\,\omega^2\varphi\big)(x)\cos\omega t = 0\) for every \(x\) and \(t\).
  3. If equation (13.47) holds, this product (shape times factor) is zero at every \(x\) and \(t\). Conversely, choose \(t = 0\): then \(EI\,\varphi''''(x) = \rho A\,\omega^2\varphi(x)\) for every \(x\), which is equation (13.47), since \(\beta\) is the positive fourth root of \(\rho A\,\omega^2/EI\).
  4. Every end condition of definition 13.39 is an equation in which the value of \(\varphi\) or of one of its derivatives at \(e\), multiplied by \(\cos\omega t\), equals zero (the ends of the blue curve stay where the support requires at all three times). By step 1 it holds at every time if and only if it holds for \(\varphi\) itself.

Source: CK (13.9) to (13.13), PDF p. 410, GR (4.245) to (4.247), PDF pp. 286 to 287: the harmonic motion is substituted into the equation of motion. The proof by steps is not from the source.

The definition requires \(\omega > 0\), that is, vibration. Could there be a motion in a constant shape whose displacement grows or stands still, which would be \(\lambda = \omega^2 \le 0\) in the equation \(EI\,\varphi'''' = \lambda\,\rho A\,\varphi\)? The lemma shows that for the three supports we compute, there cannot. Figure 13.76 shows what the proof compares. At upper left is the deflection with its ends: the blue curve \(\varphi\) above the grey dashed axis, for a simply supported example, the blackwhite dots are the ends, where at least one factor of each product is zero. Below it are the two areas, the blue and the orange one, above their grey axes, the integrals of \(\varphi^2\) and \(\varphi''^2\) (for a sine of the same shape). Both are nonnegative and not zero, so their quotient \(\lambda\) is positive. On the right are the rigid motions: the horizontal deflection of a beam with both ends free, raised above the axis, and the slanted line of a beam simply supported at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L\), above its axis. These are rigid motions, for which \(\varphi'' = 0\) and therefore \(\lambda = 0\).

Lemma 13.41 Positive eigenvalue of a beam (pozitivna lastna vrednost nosilca)

Let \(\varphi \not\equiv 0\) be a four times continuously differentiable function on \([0, L]\) (blue deflection), \(\lambda\) a real number and \(EI\,\varphi'''' = \lambda\,\rho A\,\varphi\). Let the beam be clamped at both ends, or simply supported at both ends, or clamped at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L\), and let \(\varphi\) satisfy the end conditions of theorem 13.40. Then \(\lambda > 0\).

Proof

We must show that \(\lambda\) is the quotient of a nonnegative integral and a positive one, that is, of the orange and the blue area. We multiply the equation by \(\varphi\) and integrate over the whole beam, a statement about the interval \([0, L]\) and not about a slice.

  1. By corollary 3.56 with \(f = \varphi\) and \(g = \varphi'''\), and once more with \(f = \varphi'\) and \(g = \varphi''\),
    \[\int_0^L \varphi''''\,\varphi\,\mathrm{d}x = \Big[\varphi'''\,\varphi - \varphi''\,\varphi'\Big]_0^L + \int_0^L \varphi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  2. The bracket is zero at each end. A clamped end has \(\varphi = \varphi' = 0\), a simply supported one \(\varphi = \varphi'' = 0\), a free one \(\varphi'' = \varphi''' = 0\), and in every case both products have at least one zero factor.
  3. From the equation and step 1, \(\lambda\,\rho A \int_0^L \varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x = EI \int_0^L \varphi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). The integrand \(\varphi^2\) is continuous and nonnegative (blue area), and since \(\varphi\) is not identically zero, \(\int_0^L \varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x > 0\) (lemma 6.10, item 3). The right side is nonnegative (orange area), so \(\lambda \ge 0\).
  4. Let \(\lambda = 0\). Then \(\int_0^L \varphi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), by lemma 6.10 (item 3) \(\varphi'' = 0\) on \([0, L]\), by corollary 1.86 \(\varphi'\) is constant, and \(\varphi(x) = p + q\,x\). At a clamped end \(e\), \(\varphi'(e) = q = 0\) and \(\varphi(e) = p = 0\), so \(\varphi = 0\). For the beam simply supported at both ends, \(\varphi(0) = 0\) and \(\varphi(L) = 0\) give \(p = 0\) and \(q\,L = 0\), so again \(\varphi = 0\). This is a contradiction, so \(\lambda > 0\). The line \(p + q\,x\) would survive only for supports that allow a rigid motion, and a clamped end and two simple supports do not.

Source: The proof is not from the source. GR (table 4.3, PDF p. 289) lists the eigenvalue \(0\) for the beam with both ends free, a rigid-body motion that the lemma excludes for our three supports.

For a beam with both ends free, or with one free and one simply supported end, the lemma does not hold, because such a beam can move or rotate as a rigid body. Their modes and rigid motions are in section 13.6.9.

Two cases show where the proof of lemma 13.41 stops. For a beam with both ends free we have \(\varphi'' = \varphi''' = 0\) at both ends. The function \(\varphi = 1\) (horizontal orange line) solves \(\varphi'''' = 0 = 0 \cdot \varphi\) and both conditions at both ends, so \(\lambda = 0\) and not \(\lambda > 0\). For a beam simply supported at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L\), such a solution is \(\varphi = x\) (slanted orange line): \(\varphi(0) = \varphi''(0) = 0\) and \(\varphi''(L) = \varphi'''(L) = 0\). These are a rigid translation and a rigid rotation about the support. Steps 1 to 3 of the proof hold here, since the square bracket is zero at every end, and in both cases \(\int_0^L \varphi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\), which in step 3 is exactly what gives \(\lambda = 0\). The difference is in step 4: from \(\varphi'' = 0\) it follows that \(\varphi = p + q\,x\), and with a clamped end or with simple supports at both ends the conditions give \(p = q = 0\). In these two cases \(p\) and \(q\) are arbitrary. The lemma therefore requires supports that prevent rigid motion.

13.6.2 Ends with elements

The end of a real beam is seldom one of the three kinds of definition 13.39. The beam of a machine stands on a spring, carries a motor or a sensor at its end, and a damper holds it at the support. What holds at the end then? The answer is already in theorem 13.37: if the surroundings act on the end \(x = L\) with a force \(f_{\mathrm{L}}\) and a moment \(\mu_{\mathrm{L}}\), the natural conditions are \(V(L, t) = f_{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(M(L, t) = \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\). We only have to say how large the force and the moment of each element are.

Figure 13.77 shows six right ends. In each, the grey dashed line is the axis before bending and the blue curve is the beam, which continues to the left. The first is the general end: the end of the beam is displaced by \(w\), and the surroundings act on it with the force \(f_{\mathrm{L}}\) in the direction of the deflection and the moment \(\mu_{\mathrm{L}}\) in the direction of the slope. At the sliding end the end is fixed to a slider that runs without friction along a vertical guide: the guide allows no rotation and does not hinder the displacement. At the spring the end is tied to the ground by a coil spring of stiffness \(k\). When the end rises by \(w\), the spring is stretched by that much and pulls the end back with the force \(k\,w\), so \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = -k\,w\). The rotational spring of stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) resists the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) with the moment \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \(\mu_{\mathrm{L}} = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). At the mass a small rigid body with mass \(m\) and moment of inertia \(J_0\) about the axis perpendicular to the plane of bending is fixed to the end. The beam accelerates the body, and by the law of action and reaction the body acts back with the opposite force, \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) (the arrow in the figure holds for an upward acceleration). At the damper the end moves with the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the viscous damper (definition 9.1) resists with the force \(c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\) against the velocity, \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\). Next to each end are the two conditions that we prove.

Definition 13.42 Sliding end and end with an element (drsni konec in konec z elementom)

Let \(e\) be one of the ends \(0\) or \(L\) of a beam with deflection \(w(x, t)\), as in figure 13.77.

  • The end \(e\) is sliding (drsni, also guided) if the slope is prescribed, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t) = 0\) at every time \(t\), while the displacement \(w(e, t)\) is not prescribed and no transverse force acts on the end.
  • The end \(e\) has a spring of stiffness \(k > 0\) (unit N/m) if the force \(f_{\mathrm{e}} = -k\,w(e, t)\) acts on it.
  • The end \(e\) has a rotational spring of stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\) (unit N m per radian) if the moment \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}} = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t)\) acts on it.
  • The end \(e\) has a mass \(m > 0\) with moment of inertia \(J_0 \ge 0\) if a rigid body that moves with the end is fixed to it. For \(J_0 = 0\) it is a point mass.
  • The end \(e\) has a damper with coefficient \(c > 0\) (unit N s/m) if the force \(f_{\mathrm{e}} = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(e, t)\) acts on it.

The force \(f_{\mathrm{e}}\) is positive in the direction of the deflection \(w\), the moment \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\) in the direction of increasing slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), as in theorem 13.37.

Source: The forces of the elements are written by theorem 13.37. The mass at the end is treated in CK example 12.3. The other ends are not from a source (source needed).

In the lectures the simply supported end is called a pinned end (členkasto podprt konec) and the damper dušilka. The deflection \(w\) points down there and the shear force is written \(T\). The conditions of the theorem that follows are all equations in which every term has exactly one \(w\) or one of its derivatives. The change \(w \to -w\) therefore multiplies both sides by \(-1\) and does not change a condition: the table holds for both directions of the deflection. The sign depends only on whether the end is the left or the right one.

Theorem 13.43 Conditions at ends with elements (pogoji koncev z elementi)

Let the beam be as in theorem 13.37, with constant \(EI\), \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(V = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\), and let an end have an element of definition 13.42. Then for the motion of the beam the two conditions of the table hold at every time (the conditions next to each end of the figure are the column for \(x = L\)).

end force and moment of the element conditions at \(x = L\) conditions at \(x = 0\) kind term in the action
sliding none \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\) \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\) essential, natural none
spring \(k\) \(f = -k\,w\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = k\,w\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = -k\,w\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) natural \(-\tfrac12 k\,w(e, t)^2\)
rotational spring \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) \(\mu = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\) natural \(-\tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t)^2\)
point mass \(m\) \(f = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) natural \(+\tfrac12 m\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(e, t)^2\)
mass \(m\) with \(J_0\) \(f = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(\mu = -J_0\,w_{\mathrm{xtt}}\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -J_0\,w_{\mathrm{xtt}}\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = J_0\,w_{\mathrm{xtt}}\) natural \(+\tfrac12 m\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \tfrac12 J_0\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}^2\)
damper \(c\) \(f = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) natural none, the force is not conservative

If the beam vibrates in a mode \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\), the conditions for \(\varphi\) at \(x = L\) read: spring \(EI\,\varphi''' = k\,\varphi\), rotational spring \(EI\,\varphi'' = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,\varphi'\), mass \(EI\,\varphi''' = -m\,\omega^2\varphi\) and \(EI\,\varphi'' = J_0\,\omega^2\varphi'\). At \(x = 0\) the right sides have the opposite sign.

Proof

We must show that every condition follows from the natural conditions of theorem 13.37 when the force and moment of the element are put into them (the orange arrows of the figure).

  1. The natural conditions (13.43) are \(V(L, t) = f_{\mathrm{L}}\), \(M(L, t) = \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\), \(V(0, t) = -f_0\) and \(M(0, t) = -\mu_0\) (the general end). With \(V = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\) and \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) this is \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = -f_{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mu_{\mathrm{L}}\) at \(x = L\), and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = f_0\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\mu_0\) at \(x = 0\). The signs at the left end are opposite because \(V\) is the force on the face with outward normal along \(+x\), and the left end has its outward normal along \(-x\).
  2. Spring: the spring is stretched by the displacement \(w(e, t)\) and pulls toward its unstretched position, \(f_{\mathrm{e}} = -k\,w(e, t)\). Step 1 gives \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}(L, t) = k\,w(L, t)\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}(0, t) = -k\,w(0, t)\). There is no moment, so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\).
  3. Rotational spring: the moment is \(\mu_{\mathrm{e}} = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t)\), against the slope. Step 1 gives \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(L, t) = -k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(0, t) = k_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t)\). There is no force, so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\).
  4. Mass: the beam acts on the body with the force \(-f_{\mathrm{e}}\) and the moment \(-\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\) (law of action and reaction). The body has the acceleration \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}(e, t)\) and, being rigidly fixed to the end, the rotation \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(e, t)\). Newton's second law for the body gives \(m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -f_{\mathrm{e}}\), and the law of angular momentum about the axis through the end gives \(J_0\,w_{\mathrm{xtt}} = -\mu_{\mathrm{e}}\). Step 1 gives the conditions of the table.
  5. Damper: by definition 9.1 the force is opposite to the velocity, \(f_{\mathrm{e}} = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(e, t)\), and step 1 gives \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}(L, t) = c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)\) and \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}(0, t) = -c\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(0, t)\).
  6. Sliding end: the slope is prescribed, so there is no condition on the moment (the guide takes any moment). The displacement is not prescribed and there is no force, \(f_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\), so \(V = 0\), that is \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}} = 0\).
  7. The term in the action. The spring has the potential energy \(\tfrac12 k\,w(L, t)^2\), which is subtracted in the action (13.41). Its variation is \(-k\,w(L, t)\,\eta(L, t)\), which is the term \(f_{\mathrm{L}}\,\eta(L, t)\) with \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = -k\,w\). The mass has the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12 m\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2\). The variation of its time integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} m\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t = -\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}t\) by corollary 3.56, because \(\eta(L, t_1) = \eta(L, t_2) = 0\). This is the term \(f_{\mathrm{L}}\,\eta\) with \(f_{\mathrm{L}} = -m\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\). The same holds for \(J_0\) and \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) with \(\eta_{\mathrm{x}}\) in place of \(\eta\). The force of the damper removes energy and does not store it, so it has no term in the action and enters as the work of a nonconservative force (equation (8.127)).
  8. Mode: for \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) (shape times time factor) we have \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2\varphi\cos\omega t\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xtt}} = -\omega^2\varphi'\cos\omega t\). Putting this into the table and cancelling \(\cos\omega t\), which is not zero everywhere (theorem 13.40, step 1), gives the conditions for \(\varphi\).

Source: CK example 12.3 derives the condition of an end with a mass. The natural conditions are from theorem 13.37, the proof in steps is not from a source.

Three remarks show what the theorem assumes. First, the body at the end with a mass is small compared with the length of the beam, so that we may fix it at one point. For a body of length \(a\) with its centre of mass \(a/2\) beyond the end, the conditions would have one more term with \(m\,a/2\), which is absent here. Second, the spring and the damper have no mass. Third, the damper does not allow a motion of the form \(\varphi(x)\cos\omega t\): the condition \(EI\,\varphi'''(L)\cos\omega t = -c\,\omega\,\varphi(L)\sin\omega t\) would have to hold at every time, which requires \(\varphi'''(L) = 0\) and \(\varphi(L) = 0\) together with \(\varphi''(L) = 0\), three conditions at one end. A vibration with a damper decays and is treated in chapter 20.

We check the sign in the table with the energy. We multiply the equation \(EI\,\varphi'''' = \lambda\,\rho A\,\varphi\) by \(\varphi\) and integrate as in lemma 13.41. For a beam clamped at \(x = 0\) with a spring at \(x = L\) the boundary term is \(EI\,\varphi'''(L)\,\varphi(L) = k\,\varphi(L)^2\), so

\[\lambda\,\rho A \int_0^L \varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x = EI \int_0^L \varphi''^2\,\mathrm{d}x + k\,\varphi(L)^2 . \tag{13.48}\]

The right side is a sum of two nonnegative terms, the bending energy of the beam and the energy of the spring, as it must be. With the wrong sign of the condition the energy of the spring would be subtracted and the spring would lower the frequency. This is a test that works for every sign convention: the right condition is the one for which the spring enters this equation with a plus.

13.6.3 The general solution

The equation \(\varphi'''' = \beta^4\,\varphi\) is an ordinary differential equation (definition 5.45) of fourth order. We know four solutions (four curves): by theorem 8.13 and lemma 9.47 (item 1) the fourth derivative of each of the functions \(\cos\beta x\), \(\sin\beta x\), \(\operatorname{cosh}\beta x\) and \(\operatorname{sinh}\beta x\) equals \(\beta^4\) times the function. The lemma says that the other solutions are already their linear combinations.

Figure 13.78 shows the four functions for \(\beta = 1\). On the left the cosine and the sine are blue, the first solid and the second dashed. They oscillate, so they resemble the modes of the string. The hyperbolic cosine and the hyperbolic sine are orange, solid and dashed, and grow without oscillating. The labels at the ends of the curves say which is which. All four start on the vertical axis, where \(x = 0\), and have four different values of the derivatives there. In the middle, on their own axes, is a pair of curves, the blue function \(\varphi\) and the orange dashed combination, which have the same starting point with the same derivatives and therefore lie one on the other. On the right is the third graph: on the axis lies the blue line, the quantity of step 4 of the proof, which is zero when the two curves are equal. It starts at zero and must stay on the axis because the band above and below it is forbidden.

Lemma 13.44 All solutions of the fourth order equation (vse rešitve enačbe četrtega reda)

Let \(\beta > 0\). Every four times differentiable function \(\varphi\) on \([0, L]\) with \(\varphi'''' = \beta^4\,\varphi\) is a sum of four curves of the form

\[\begin{aligned} \varphi(x) &= C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x \\ &\quad + C_3\operatorname{cosh}\beta x + C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta x \quad \text{on } [0, L] , \end{aligned} \tag{13.49}\]

with numbers \(C_1\) to \(C_4\), and every such function is a solution.

Proof

We must show that for given values \(\varphi(0)\), \(\varphi'(0)\), \(\varphi''(0)\), \(\varphi'''(0)\) there are numbers \(C_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the same values, and that the equation with zero initial values has only the zero solution, that is, two solutions with the same starting point and the same derivatives coincide (middle of the figure).

  1. Every function of the form (13.49) is a solution (a sum of four curves), because the equation is linear and all four terms solve it.
  2. The values \((f, f', f'', f''')\) at \(0\) (vertical axis of the figure) are \((1, 0, -\beta^2, 0)\) for \(\cos\beta x\), \((0, \beta, 0, -\beta^3)\) for \(\sin\beta x\), \((1, 0, \beta^2, 0)\) for \(\operatorname{cosh}\beta x\) and \((0, \beta, 0, \beta^3)\) for \(\operatorname{sinh}\beta x\) (theorem 8.13, lemma 9.47, items 1 and 2). We choose
    \[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \tfrac12\Big(\varphi(0) - \frac{\varphi''(0)}{\beta^2}\Big), & C_3 &= \tfrac12\Big(\varphi(0) + \frac{\varphi''(0)}{\beta^2}\Big), \\ C_2 &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\varphi'(0)}{\beta} - \frac{\varphi'''(0)}{\beta^3}\Big), & C_4 &= \tfrac12\Big(\frac{\varphi'(0)}{\beta} + \frac{\varphi'''(0)}{\beta^3}\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
    Substitution gives \(C_1 + C_3 = \varphi(0)\), \(\beta^2(C_3 - C_1) = \varphi''(0)\), \(\beta(C_2 + C_4) = \varphi'(0)\) and \(\beta^3(C_4 - C_2) = \varphi'''(0)\), so the function (13.49) has the same initial values as \(\varphi\).
  3. Let \(\psi\) be the difference of \(\varphi\) and this function, that is, of the two curves in the middle of the figure. It is a solution (step 1), so \(\psi'''' = \beta^4\psi\) with zero initial values. Let \(S = \psi^2 + \psi'^2 + \psi''^2 + \psi'''^2\). The function \(S\) is differentiable and \(S' = 2\psi\psi' + 2\psi'\psi'' + 2\psi''\psi''' + 2\beta^4\psi\psi'''\). Since \(2uv \le u^2 + v^2\) (from \((u - v)^2 \ge 0\)), \(S' \le (1 + \beta^8)\,\psi^2 + 2\psi'^2 + 2\psi''^2 + 2\psi'''^2 \le K\,S\) with \(K = 2 + \beta^8\).
  4. The function \(\mathrm{e}^{-Kx}\,S(x)\) has derivative \(\mathrm{e}^{-Kx}(S' - K\,S) \le 0\) (theorem 9.18, item 2), so by theorem 1.85 it is nonincreasing: it cannot enter the upper band. Its value at \(0\) is \(S(0) = 0\), so \(\mathrm{e}^{-Kx} S(x) \le 0\) for every \(x\), and since \(S \ge 0\), it cannot enter the lower band, so it lies on the axis and \(S = 0\). So \(\psi = 0\), which means the blue and the orange curve coincide, and \(\varphi\) is the function (13.49).

Source: CK (13.14), PDF p. 410: the general solution is written without a proof that there is no other. The proof by steps is not from the source.

The end conditions give a homogeneous system for the numbers \(C_{\mathrm{i}}\). We shall need a system of two equations in two unknowns twice, so we solve it in advance. Figure 13.79 shows it in the \((C_1, C_2)\) plane with the axes \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). Each equation is a line through the origin, because the pair \((0, 0)\) is always a solution. On the left the blue and the orange line are different (the numbers \(A_{11}, A_{12}, A_{21}, A_{22}\) are \(2, 1, 1, 3\)), so they meet only at the origin and there is no nonzero solution. In the middle the second pair of equations (\(2, 1, 4, 2\)) gives the same blue line, covered by the orange dashed one, so the solutions are all points on it, the origin included. The arrow shows the direction of this line, \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\). On the right is the case in which the first equation is empty: one orange line remains, since both \(A\) of the first row are zero.

Lemma 13.45 Homogeneous system of two equations (homogen sistem dveh enačb)

Let \(A_{11}\), \(A_{12}\), \(A_{21}\), \(A_{22}\) be real numbers and \((A_{11}, A_{12}) \ne (0, 0)\), as in the first two cases of the figure. The system \(A_{11}\,C_1 + A_{12}\,C_2 = 0\), \(A_{21}\,C_1 + A_{22}\,C_2 = 0\) has a nonzero solution \((C_1, C_2)\) if and only if \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21} = 0\), and then all solutions are multiples of the pair \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\).

Proof

We must show that the condition is necessary and sufficient and that the solutions are multiples, that is, that they all lie on the line with direction \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\).

  1. Let \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21} = 0\), which is the middle case of the figure. The pair \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\) is not zero because \((A_{11}, A_{12}) \ne (0, 0)\). It solves the first equation, \(A_{11}A_{12} - A_{12}A_{11} = 0\), and the second, \(A_{21}A_{12} - A_{22}A_{11} = -(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21}) = 0\).
  2. Let \((C_1, C_2) \ne (0, 0)\) be a solution, that is, a point other than the origin on both lines. We multiply the first equation by \(A_{22}\), the second by \(A_{12}\) and subtract: \((A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21})\,C_1 = 0\). We multiply the first by \(A_{21}\), the second by \(A_{11}\) and subtract: \((A_{12}A_{21} - A_{11}A_{22})\,C_2 = 0\). One of \(C_1\), \(C_2\) is not zero, so \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21} = 0\).
  3. Let this determinant be zero and \((C_1, C_2)\) a solution, that is, a point on the common line. The first equation says \(A_{11}\,C_1 = -A_{12}\,C_2\). If \(A_{11} \ne 0\), then \((C_1, C_2) = (C_2/A_{11})\,(-A_{12}, A_{11})\), a multiple of the pair \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\). If \(A_{11} = 0\), then \(A_{12} \ne 0\), so \(C_2 = 0\) and \((C_1, C_2) = (C_1/A_{12})\,(A_{12}, 0)\), again a multiple.

Source: The proof is not from the source.

In the computations we also need two estimates, shown in figure 13.80. The solid orange curve is \(\cosh t\), the dashed orange one is \(\sinh t\), the grey dashed line is the height \(1\), and the labels beside them say which is which. The first lies above the height \(1\) for \(t > 0\), the second above the horizontal axis \(t\), and the gap between them is \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\), which is not zero. For \(t > 0\), by theorem 9.18 (item 1) \(\mathrm{e}^{2t} > 1\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{t} \ne 1\), so

\[\operatorname{sinh}t = \tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{-t}\big(\mathrm{e}^{2t} - 1\big) > 0 , \qquad \operatorname{cosh}t = 1 + \tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{-t}\big(\mathrm{e}^{t} - 1\big)^2 > 1 . \tag{13.50}\]

Also \(\operatorname{cosh}t > \operatorname{sinh}t\), so the solid curve lies above the dashed one, because \(\operatorname{cosh}t - \operatorname{sinh}t = \mathrm{e}^{-t} > 0\) (theorem 9.18, item 1). The functions \(\operatorname{sinh}\) and \(\operatorname{cosh}\) are increasing on \([0, \infty)\) because their derivatives \(\operatorname{cosh}\) and \(\operatorname{sinh}\) are nonnegative (lemma 9.47, items 1 and 3, and theorem 1.85). We write \(\operatorname{sech}t = 1/\operatorname{cosh}t\).

The condition \((A_{11}, A_{12}) \ne (0, 0)\) of lemma 13.45 is not decoration. Take \(A_{11} = A_{12} = 0\) and \(A_{21} = A_{22} = 1\), which is the right case of the figure. The determinant is \(0 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 1 = 0\), but the solutions are all pairs with \(C_1 + C_2 = 0\), that is \(t\,(1, -1)\) with arbitrary \(t\). These are not multiples of \((A_{12}, -A_{11}) = (0, 0)\), because multiples of the zero pair are zero themselves, and the zero pair is only the origin. The first equation is empty here (\(0 = 0\)) and step 1 of the proof fails, since the pair \((A_{12}, -A_{11})\) is not nonzero. This is why we will check, for the cantilever in step 3 of theorem 13.52, that for every \(x > 0\) at least one of the numbers \(A_{11}\), \(A_{12}\) differs from zero.

13.6.4 The simply supported beam

The simplest case is a beam simply supported at both ends. The shape is the same as for the string, the reason is different: the sine is here a solution of the fourth order equation because its second derivative is zero where it is zero itself. Figure 13.81 shows the first three modes. Each row has the grey dashed axis, the triangular supports at the ends and the blue deflection, a sine with \(k\) half waves, and beside the row is the label \(k\). On the right is an orange bar for the frequency, with a length proportional to it.

Theorem 13.46 Modes of a simply supported beam (načini prostoležečega nosilca)

Let a uniform beam be simply supported at both ends. A pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) with \(\omega > 0\) is a mode if and only if \(\beta L = k\pi\) with an integer \(k \ge 1\) and \(\varphi\) is a nonzero multiple of the function \(\sin(k\pi x/L)\), the blue curves of the figure. The frequencies are

\[\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{(k\pi)^2}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}} , \qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \dots \tag{13.51}\]
Proof

We must show that the conditions at \(x = 0\) remove the cosines and the conditions at \(x = L\) leave only the sine. They are the conditions of the supports at the left and the right end.

  1. By theorem 13.40 and lemma 13.44, \(\varphi = C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x + C_3\operatorname{cosh}\beta x + C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta x\), a sum of the four curves.
  2. At the left support the conditions \(\varphi(0) = C_1 + C_3 = 0\) and \(\varphi''(0) = \beta^2(C_3 - C_1) = 0\) give \(C_3 = -C_1\) and \(C_3 = C_1\), so \(C_1 = C_3 = 0\).
  3. The conditions at the right support at \(x = L\) are \(\varphi(L) = C_2\sin\beta L + C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta L = 0\) and \(\varphi''(L) = \beta^2\big({-C_2}\sin\beta L + C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta L\big) = 0\). The sum gives \(2\,\beta^2 C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta L = 0\), and since \(\operatorname{sinh}\beta L > 0\) (equation (13.50)), \(C_4 = 0\).
  4. What remains is \(C_2\sin\beta L = 0\). Since \(\varphi \ne 0\), steps 2 and 3 give \(C_2 \ne 0\), so \(\sin\beta L = 0\), that is, the blue curve has a zero at the right support. By lemma 8.11 (items 3 and 4) the sine is positive on \((0, \pi)\), negative on \((-\pi, 0)\) and periodic with period \(2\pi\), so \(\sin\theta = 0\) only at multiples of \(\pi\). Since \(\beta L > 0\), \(\beta L = k\pi\) with \(k \ge 1\).
  5. Conversely, for \(\beta = k\pi/L\) (the three modes of the figure) the function \(\varphi = \sin\beta x\) satisfies \(\varphi'''' = \beta^4\varphi\) (step 1 of lemma 13.44), \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\), and \(\varphi'' = -\beta^2\varphi\) is zero at both ends. By theorem 13.40 it is a mode.
  6. From \(\beta^4 = \rho A\,\omega^2/EI\) we get \(\omega = \beta^2\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)}\), which is equation (13.51) and the length of the orange bars.

Source: CK example 13.2, PDF pp. 411 to 413: equation (9) on p. 412, \(\sin\lambda L = 0\), and figure 2 on p. 413. GR table 4.3, PDF p. 289, row bipinned: \(\mu_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi\). The proof by steps is not from the source.

At \(L = 1\) m and the beam of the introduction, \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{EI/(\rho A L^4)} = 57{,}883\) 1/s and \(\omega_{\mathrm{k}} = (k\pi)^2\,\omega_0\). The frequencies \(f_{\mathrm{k}} = \omega_{\mathrm{k}}/(2\pi)\) are \(90{,}92\), \(363{,}69\) and \(818{,}30\) Hz for \(k = 1, 2, 3\). The second is \(4\) times and the third \(9\) times the first (the bars are \(4\) times and \(9\) times as long), because the frequency is proportional to the square of the wave number \(\beta\): a wave half as long gives a frequency four times as high. For the string it was proportional to \(\beta\).

The sine is the mode shape of the string and the mode shape of the simply supported beam. So the two stiffnesses can be combined: a wire that is tensioned and also resists bending has the same shapes, and the frequencies add by their squares.

Figure 13.82 gathers this in one drawing. On the left is the wire, simply supported at both ends, tensioned with the force \(T\) and vibrating in a sinusoidal shape. In the middle is a piece of wire with two transverse forces, the tension force and the bending force. On the right are three bars for four modes: the string frequency, the beam frequency and the total frequency.

Example 13.47 A tensioned wire with bending stiffness and the tension from a measured frequency (napeta žica z upogibno togostjo in sila iz izmerjene frekvence)

Take the guitar string of example 13.8: a steel wire of diameter \(0{,}4\) mm, \(L = 0{,}65\) m, mass per length \(\mu = \rho A = 9{,}8018 \cdot 10^{-4}\) kg/m, tension \(T = 70\) N. Its bending stiffness is \(EI = 196 \cdot 10^9 \cdot \pi\,(0{,}4 \cdot 10^{-3})^4/64 = 2{,}463 \cdot 10^{-4}\) N m². The ends are simply supported: no displacement, no moment.

  1. Forces on a piece. On a piece of the wire act the transverse force of the tension, per unit length \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (theorem 13.3), and the transverse force of bending, per unit length \(-EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\) (lemma 13.38). The piece is the same, so by Newton's second law the forces add: \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\).
  2. Mode. We insert \(w = \sin(n\pi x/L)\cos\omega t\), the blue deflection of figure 13.81 with \(n\) half waves, which meets the conditions of both supports. Each double derivative in \(x\) multiplies the sine by \(-(n\pi/L)^2\), so
    \[\mu\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = T\Big(\frac{n\pi}{L}\Big)^2 + EI\Big(\frac{n\pi}{L}\Big)^4 , \qquad f_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{s}}^2 + f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{u}}^2 . \tag{13.52}\]
    Here \(f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}\) is the frequency of the string without bending stiffness (equation (13.6)) and \(f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{u}} = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}(n\pi/L)^2\sqrt{EI/\mu}\) the frequency of the simply supported beam without tension (equation (13.51)). The square of the frequency is the sum of the squares of the two.
  3. Numbers (mpmath).
\(n\) \(f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{s}}\) [Hz] \(f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{u}}\) [Hz] \(f_{\mathrm{n}}\) [Hz] difference from the string
\(1\) \(205{,}567\) \(1{,}864\) \(205{,}575\) \(0{,}004\) %
\(3\) \(616{,}70\) \(16{,}77\) \(616{,}93\) \(0{,}04\) %
\(10\) \(2055{,}7\) \(186{,}4\) \(2064{,}1\) \(0{,}41\) %
\(20\) \(4111{,}3\) \(745{,}5\) \(4178{,}4\) \(1{,}6\) %

The share of bending grows with \(n^2\) (the bars of the beam grow with \(n^2\), the frequencies of the string only with \(n\)), so the high modes of a stiff wire lie above the whole multiples of the first. 4. Tension from the frequency. For \(n = 1\) and negligible bending (the beam bar \(f_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{u}}\) is then tiny next to the string bar), equation (13.52) gives

\[T = 4\,L^2 f_1^2\,\mu . \tag{13.53}\]

We measure \(f_1 = 205{,}575\) Hz. Then \(T = 4 \cdot 0{,}65^2 \cdot 205{,}575^2 \cdot 9{,}8018 \cdot 10^{-4} = 70{,}006\) N. Bending contributes \(0{,}006\) N: if we subtract \(f_{1,\mathrm{u}}^2 = 1{,}864^2\) from \(f_1^2\), we get \(70{,}000\) N. An error of the measured frequency counts twice: at \(207\) Hz instead of \(205{,}575\) Hz (\(0{,}7\) % more), \(T = 70{,}98\) N (\(1{,}4\) % more), because \(T\) is proportional to \(f_1^2\).

When may bending be neglected? The ratio of the two terms of equation (13.52) is \(EI\,(n\pi/L)^2/T\). For the string and \(n = 1\) it is \(8 \cdot 10^{-5}\), so equation (13.53) holds to four digits. For a belt or a steel band, which is short and thick, the ratio can be near \(1\), and the tension computed by the string equation is then too high: part of the frequency comes from bending. The moving belt with both terms is treated in chapter 26.

13.6.5 Roots of transcendental equations

For the cantilever and the beam clamped at both ends we shall obtain the equations \(\cos x\operatorname{cosh}x = -1\) and \(\cos x\operatorname{cosh}x = 1\) for \(x = \beta L > 0\). There is no closed formula for the roots, CK (p. 414) gives a table and GR (p. 288) an iterative computation. Before computing, we show that the roots exist and place them in intervals. Figure 13.83 shows the idea: we write the equations as \(\cos x = \mp\operatorname{sech}x\). The upper graph is the equation \(\cos x = -\operatorname{sech}x\) of the cantilever, the lower one is the equation \(\cos x = \operatorname{sech}x\) of the beam clamped at both ends. In both, the horizontal axis is the value \(x = \beta L\), marked at multiples of \(\pi/2\), because the zeros and peaks of the cosine are there. The blue curve is \(\cos x\), the upper orange one is \(-\operatorname{sech}x\), the lower orange one is \(\operatorname{sech}x\). Where a blue and an orange curve cross there is a blackwhite dot, a root of the equation. The function \(\operatorname{sech}x\) is smaller than \(0{,}09\) for \(x \ge \pi\), so the cosine meets its graph right beside its own zeros.

The figure shows that in each band where the cosine has the right sign it meets the orange curve twice, once on each side of the middle of the band, in two dots. The lemma proves this. Figure 13.84 enlarges one band for \(n = 1\). At the top are the blue curve \(\cos y\) and the orange one \(\operatorname{sech}(n\pi + y)\) on the band between the ends \(\pm\pi/2\) of the horizontal axis \(y\). The left dot and the right dot are the solutions. At \(y = 0\) there is a gap between the curves, since the cosine is \(1\) and sech is small. In the middle are the blue \(g(s)\) and the orange \(g_+(s)\) for \(s \ge 0\) above the axis \(s\), the differences for the left and the right half. Both decrease and each has one zero. At the bottom, on the axis \(y\), is the case \(n = 0\), where the blue and the orange dashed curve touch at a dot and do not cross.

Lemma 13.48 Roots of the frequency equation of the cantilever (korenine frekvenčne enačbe konzole)

Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer. The equation \(\cos y = \operatorname{sech}(n\pi + y)\) (the upper band of the figure) has exactly two solutions in the interval \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\), one in \((-\pi/2, 0)\) and one in \((0, \pi/2)\).

Proof

We must show that each half of the interval contains a solution (theorem 2.79, the dots) and that there is only one on it (strictly monotone difference, decreasing curves). At \(y = 0\) there is no solution (the gap in the figure) because \(\cos 0 = 1 > \operatorname{sech}(n\pi)\) by equation (13.50). We use the numerical values \(\operatorname{sech}\pi = 0{,}08627\), \(\sin 0{,}1 = 0{,}09983\) and \(\cos 0{,}1 = 0{,}9950\) (mpmath). The decisive inequality is \(\sin 0{,}1 > \operatorname{sech}\pi\) in step 5. The margin \(0{,}0136\) is more than a thousand times the rounding \(5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the bound for \(\operatorname{sech}\pi\) also follows without a computer: from \(\mathrm{e}^\pi > 23\), \(\operatorname{sech}\pi = 2/(\mathrm{e}^\pi + \mathrm{e}^{-\pi}) < 2\,\mathrm{e}^{-\pi} < 2/23 < 0{,}087\).

  1. Left half: let \(y = -s\) and \(g(s) = \cos s - \operatorname{sech}(n\pi - s)\) on \([0, \pi/2]\), where \(u = n\pi - s \ge n\pi - \pi/2 > 0\). The derivative of \(\operatorname{sech}\) is \(-\operatorname{sinh}/\operatorname{cosh}^2\) (lemma 9.47, item 1, and the quotient rule), so \(g'(s) = -\sin s - \operatorname{sech}u\,\tanh u\) with \(\tanh u = \operatorname{sinh}u/\operatorname{cosh}u > 0\) (equation (13.50)). On \((0, \pi/2]\), \(\sin s > 0\) (lemma 8.11, item 3), so \(g' < 0\) and \(g\) is strictly decreasing by theorem 1.85 (the blue curve).
  2. Values: \(g(0) = 1 - \operatorname{sech}(n\pi) > 0\) and \(g(\pi/2) = -\operatorname{sech}(n\pi - \pi/2) < 0\). By theorem 2.79 there is a zero in \((0, \pi/2)\) (the blue dot), by step 1 only one.
  3. Right half: let \(g_+(s) = \cos s - \operatorname{sech}(n\pi + s)\) on \([0, \pi/2]\). Again \(g_+(0) > 0\) and \(g_+(\pi/2) = -\operatorname{sech}(n\pi + \pi/2) < 0\), so by theorem 2.79 a zero in \((0, \pi/2)\) exists (the orange curve crosses the axis).
  4. On \([0, 0{,}1]\) (the grey segment) there is no zero: the cosine is decreasing there (lemma 8.11, item 3), so \(\cos s \ge \cos 0{,}1 = 0{,}9950\), while \(\operatorname{sech}(n\pi + s) \le \operatorname{sech}\pi = 0{,}08627\) because \(\operatorname{cosh}\) is increasing.
  5. On \([0{,}1, \pi/2)\), \(g_+'(s) = -\sin s + \operatorname{sech}x\,\tanh x\) with \(x = n\pi + s\). The sine is increasing here because its derivative \(\cos > 0\) (theorem 1.85), so \(\sin s \ge \sin 0{,}1 = 0{,}09983\). At the same time \(\operatorname{sech}x\,\tanh x < \operatorname{sech}x \le \operatorname{sech}\pi = 0{,}08627\), because \(\tanh x < 1\) (equation (13.50)) and \(x \ge \pi\). So \(g_+' < 0\), \(g_+\) (the orange curve) is strictly decreasing on \([0{,}1, \pi/2)\) and has at most one zero there. Together with steps 3 and 4 the zero is unique.

Source: The proof is not from the source. GR (p. 288, figure 4.26) shows the root of the cantilever as an intersection of two curves and an iterative computation, and does not prove the existence or the number of roots.

The condition \(n \ge 1\) in the lemma is necessary, as the lower band of the figure shows. For \(n = 0\) the equation reads \(\cos y = \operatorname{sech}y\) and the difference \(g(s) = \cos s - \operatorname{sech}s\) has the value \(0\) at \(s = 0\), not the positive value \(1 - \operatorname{sech}(n\pi)\) of step 2. The expansions \(\cos s = 1 - s^2/2 + s^4/24 - \dots\) and \(\operatorname{sech}s = 1 - s^2/2 + 5\,s^4/24 - \dots\) give \(g(s) \approx -s^4/6\). Numerically \(g(0{,}1) = -1{,}66 \cdot 10^{-5}\), \(g(0{,}5) = -0{,}00924\), \(g(1) = -0{,}1078\) and \(g(1{,}5) = -0{,}3544\), and \(g\) is not positive at any of \(20\,001\) tested points of \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\). The cosine only touches the curve \(\operatorname{sech}\) at \(y = 0\) (the blackwhite dot) and does not cross it: one double zero instead of one zero on each side. For \(n \ge 1\) the cosine is above the curve at \(y = 0\) (\(1\) against \(\operatorname{sech}(n\pi) \le 0{,}08627\)) and crosses it once on each side.

Beams with one simply supported end (section 13.6.9) give a third equation, \(\tan x = \tanh x\). Multiplied by \(\cos x\operatorname{cosh}x\) it reads \(\sin x\operatorname{cosh}x - \cos x\operatorname{sinh}x = 0\), and divided by \(\operatorname{cosh}x > 0\) it reads \(\cos x\tanh x - \sin x = 0\). Figure 13.85 shows this last form. At the top, above the \(x\) axis marked at the multiples of \(\pi\), is the blue curve \(u(x) = \cos x\tanh x - \sin x\). The curve starts at the origin, goes down and first crosses the axis only after \(\pi\). The grey segments of the axis are the intervals \([m\pi,\ m\pi + \pi/4]\) for \(m = 1, 2, 3, 4\). In each lies one blackwhite dot, a root, just before the right end of the segment. Why there? For large \(x\), \(\tanh x\) is almost \(1\), the equation is almost \(\tan x = 1\), and that one has the solutions \(m\pi + \pi/4\).

Lemma 13.49 Roots of the equation tan x = tanh x (korenine enačbe tan x = tanh x)

Let \(h(x) = \sin x\operatorname{cosh}x - \cos x\operatorname{sinh}x\) for real \(x\). Then \(h(0) = 0\), on \((0, \pi]\) we have \(h > 0\), and for every integer \(m \ge 1\) the function \(h\) has exactly one zero on the interval \([m\pi,\ (m + 1)\pi]\). It lies in \(\big(m\pi,\ m\pi + \pi/4\big)\), the grey segment of figure 13.85. The first four zeros are \(3{,}9266\), \(7{,}0686\), \(10{,}2102\) and \(13{,}3518\).

Proof

We must show that \(h\) is strictly monotone on the first half of each interval and has opposite signs at the ends of the grey segment, and that it has no zero on the second half. The blue curve is \(u = -h/\operatorname{cosh}\) and has the same zeros as \(h\), because \(\operatorname{cosh}x > 1\) (equation (13.50)).

  1. Derivative: \(h'(x) = \cos x\operatorname{cosh}x + \sin x\operatorname{sinh}x + \sin x\operatorname{sinh}x - \cos x\operatorname{cosh}x = 2\sin x\operatorname{sinh}x\) (theorem 8.13, lemma 9.47, item 1).
  2. The interval \((0, \pi]\): there \(\sin x \ge 0\) with equality only at \(\pi\), and \(\operatorname{sinh}x > 0\), so \(h' > 0\) on \((0, \pi)\). By theorem 1.85 \(h\) is strictly increasing, and since \(h(0) = 0\), we have \(h > 0\) on \((0, \pi]\). In the figure the blue curve \(u = -h/\operatorname{cosh}\) is below the axis there.
  3. First half, \(x = m\pi + s\) with \(0 \le s \le \pi/2\): by corollary 8.16, \(\sin x = (-1)^m\sin s\) and \(\cos x = (-1)^m\cos s\). So \(h' = 2\,(-1)^m\sin s\operatorname{sinh}x\) has the sign \((-1)^m\) for \(0 < s < \pi/2\), and \(h\) is strictly monotone on \([m\pi,\ m\pi + \pi/2]\): the blue curve, which has the sign of \(-h\), crosses the axis above the grey segment at most once.
  4. The ends of the grey segment: \(h(m\pi) = -(-1)^m\operatorname{sinh}(m\pi)\) and, because \(\sin(\pi/4) = \cos(\pi/4) = \sqrt2/2\), \(h(m\pi + \pi/4) = (-1)^m\,\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\big(\operatorname{cosh}x - \operatorname{sinh}x\big) = (-1)^m\,\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) at \(x = m\pi + \pi/4\). The values have opposite signs. By theorem 2.79 there is a zero between them (the blackwhite dot), and by step 3 it is the only zero on \([m\pi,\ m\pi + \pi/2]\).
  5. Second half, \(x = m\pi + \pi/2 + s\) with \(0 \le s \le \pi/2\): here \(\sin x = (-1)^m\cos s\) and \(\cos x = -(-1)^m\sin s\), so \(h(x) = (-1)^m\big(\cos s\operatorname{cosh}x + \sin s\operatorname{sinh}x\big)\). Both terms in the bracket are nonnegative and they are not zero together, so \(h \ne 0\): the blue curve to the right of the grey segment does not cross the axis.
  6. Numerically (mpmath) for the four blackwhite dots: \(h(3{,}9266) < 0 < h(3{,}9267)\), \(h(7{,}0685) > 0 > h(7{,}0686)\), \(h(10{,}2101) < 0 < h(10{,}2102)\) and \(h(13{,}3517) > 0 > h(13{,}3518)\). By theorem 2.79 each of these intervals holds a zero, by steps 3 to 5 the only one on its \([m\pi, (m + 1)\pi]\).

Source: GR table 4.3, PDF p. 289, rows free-pinned and clamped-pinned: \(3{,}927\), \(7{,}069\), \(10{,}210\) and the approximation \((4n + 1)\pi/4\). The proof is not from a source.

The lemma also tells how near the right end of the grey segment the root is. The value \(h(m\pi + \pi/4)\) in step 4 is \(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\mathrm{e}^{-x}\), for \(m = 1\) that is \(0{,}0139\) against \(\operatorname{sinh}\pi = 11{,}55\) at the other end. The first root \(3{,}92660\) is only \(3{,}9 \cdot 10^{-4}\) away from \(5\pi/4 = 3{,}92699\), which is \(\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\) at this \(x\). The next ones are less than \(10^{-6}\) away from \(9\pi/4\), \(13\pi/4\) and \(17\pi/4\).

How do we actually compute a root? The statements \(f(3{,}9266) < 0 < f(3{,}9267)\) in the proofs of this section are the outcome of a procedure that we now define. It has three steps: we plot the function, we find an interval on which it changes sign, and we halve the interval. The lower right drawing of figure 13.85 shows the halving for the first root. The top blue segment is the starting interval between the ends \(\pi\) and \(5\pi/4\), at which \(h\) has opposite signs. At the middle of the interval we compute the sign and keep the half on which the sign still changes. That is the segment of step \(1\). In the same way we get the segments of steps \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\). Each is half as long as the one before, and all contain the root, the orange dashed line.

Definition 13.50 Bracketing a root and bisection (oklepanje korena in bisekcija)

Let \(f\) be a continuous real function on an interval \([a, b]\), \(a < b\). The interval \([a, b]\) brackets a root (oklepa koren) of \(f\) if \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, \(f(a)\,f(b) < 0\). A step of bisection (bisekcija, razpolavljanje) computes the midpoint \(c = (a + b)/2\). If \(f(c) = 0\), then \(c\) is a root and the procedure ends. Otherwise it replaces \([a, b]\) by the one of the halves \([a, c]\) and \([c, b]\) that brackets a root. Bisection is the repetition of this step, the starting interval is segment \(0\) of figure 13.85, the next ones are the segments below it.

Source: The definition is not from a source (source needed: bisection and Brent's method).

Theorem 13.51 Guarantee of bisection (jamstvo bisekcije)

Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\) and let \([a, b]\) (segment \(0\)) bracket a root (definition 13.50). Then after \(n\) steps of bisection (segments below it), unless the procedure has ended with a root at a midpoint, the interval \([a_{\mathrm{n}}, b_{\mathrm{n}}]\) brackets a root, has the length

\[b_{\mathrm{n}} - a_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{b - a}{2^n} \tag{13.54}\]

and contains at least one root of \(f\). The midpoint of this interval is at most \((b - a)/2^{n+1}\) away from some root.

Proof

We must show that every step keeps the bracketing and halves the length (the segments of figure 13.85, each half as long).

  1. Let \([a, b]\) (segment \(0\)) bracket a root and let \(f(c) \ne 0\) at the midpoint \(c\). The numbers \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, and \(f(c)\) has the sign of one of them. So \(f(c)\) has the opposite sign to exactly one of the numbers \(f(a)\), \(f(b)\), and exactly one of the halves \([a, c]\), \([c, b]\) brackets a root (segment of step \(1\) is one of them). The step is therefore determined.
  2. The new half has the length \((b - a)/2\). After \(n\) steps the length is \((b - a)/2^n\), which is equation (13.54) (the segments of steps \(0\) to \(4\)).
  3. On \([a_{\mathrm{n}}, b_{\mathrm{n}}]\) the function \(f\) is continuous and has opposite signs at the ends. By theorem 2.79 it has a zero there (the orange dashed line lies in all segments). This zero is at most half the length of the interval away from the midpoint.

Source: The proof follows from theorem 2.79 and is not from a source (source needed).

On the example: \(h(\pi) = -\operatorname{sinh}\pi < 0\) and \(h(5\pi/4) > 0\) by lemma 13.49, so \([\pi, 5\pi/4]\) brackets a root. The length \(\pi/4 = 0{,}785\) shrinks to \(0{,}049\) after four steps and the interval is \([3{,}8779,\ 3{,}9270]\) (segment \(4\)). After \(10\) steps it is \([3{,}92622,\ 3{,}92699]\), after \(20\) steps \([3{,}9266021,\ 3{,}9266028]\) with the length \(7{,}5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) (mpmath). For an accuracy of \(10^{-4}\) we need \(13\) steps, because \(0{,}785/2^{13} = 9{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\). Each step gives one binary digit, ten steps about three decimal ones.

The theorem has two hypotheses and both are needed. The first is continuity. The lower left drawing of figure 13.85 shows the blue curve \(\tan x - \tanh x\) above the \(x\) axis. At \(\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/2\) the tangent has a pole (there \(\cos x = 0\)) and the curve jumps from large positive to large negative values: \(\tan 1{,}5 - \tanh 1{,}5 = +13{,}2\) and \(\tan 1{,}6 - \tanh 1{,}6 = -35{,}2\). The sign changes, but there is no root. Bisection on \([1{,}5,\ 1{,}6]\) would calmly narrow down to \(\pi/2 = 1{,}5708\). The true root is the blackwhite dot, where the curve crosses the axis: \(-0{,}052\) at \(3{,}90\) and \(+0{,}048\) at \(3{,}95\). So two rules hold. We plot the function first. We split the range at the poles or, better, multiply the equation by the denominator, as we made the continuous function \(h\) of the lemma out of \(\tan x - \tanh x\). A sign change across a pole is not a root.

The second hypothesis is the change of sign. A root at which the graph only touches the axis is not found by bisection, because the sign is not different on either side. Such is the case \(n = 0\) above (the touching point of figure 13.84). In the same way we miss two roots if they lie in one step of the grid with which we look for sign changes. The step of the grid must be smaller than the smallest distance between roots, which the plot tells or, as here, a lemma that places the roots in intervals.

Bisection is reliable and slow. Programs therefore use Brent's method (Brentova metoda), which starts from the same bracketing interval, chooses the new approximation with a line or a parabola through the last points instead of the midpoint, and returns to halving whenever the interval does not shrink fast enough. The guarantee is the same, the bracketing is kept, and the number of steps is usually several times smaller. In the SciPy library this is the function brentq. The same method of bracketing stands behind the roots of the equation of the shaft with a disk (section 13.3.5) and behind all the numerical roots of this chapter.

Figure 13.86 shows one step of each kind. The blue curve has a root between the ends, where it has opposite signs. Bisection takes the midpoint of the interval, whatever the shape of the curve. Brent's method draws a line through the points at the ends and takes its crossing with the axis: if the curve is nearly straight, this is almost exactly the root, and the distance to the true root is much smaller than for the midpoint.

13.6.6 The cantilever

The cantilever is clamped at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L\), as in chapter 5. The end conditions give the frequency equation, and lemma 13.48 locates its roots.

Theorem 13.52 Modes of a cantilever beam (načini konzole)

Let a uniform beam be clamped at \(x = 0\) (the wall) and free at \(x = L\). A pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) with \(\omega > 0\) is a mode if and only if \(x = \beta L\) is a positive solution of the equation, the blackwhite dots of the upper graph of figure 13.83,

\[\cos x\,\operatorname{cosh}x + 1 = 0 \tag{13.55}\]

and \(\varphi\) is a nonzero multiple of the function (the blue curves of figure 13.87)

\[\begin{aligned} \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(x) &= \operatorname{cosh}\beta x - \cos\beta x - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\big(\operatorname{sinh}\beta x - \sin\beta x\big) , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}} &= \frac{\operatorname{cosh}x_{\mathrm{r}} + \cos x_{\mathrm{r}}}{\operatorname{sinh}x_{\mathrm{r}} + \sin x_{\mathrm{r}}} , \end{aligned} \tag{13.56}\]

where \(x_{\mathrm{r}} = \beta L\) is that solution. There are infinitely many positive solutions, \(x_1 < x_2 < \dots\). On each interval \(\big((4m - 3)\pi/2,\ (4m - 1)\pi/2\big)\), \(m = 1, 2, \dots\), there are exactly two, one on each side of the point \((2m - 1)\pi\), and there are none elsewhere. The frequencies are \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = x_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\omega_0\) with \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{EI/(\rho A L^4)}\). The first four roots are \(x_1 = 1{,}8751\), \(x_2 = 4{,}6941\), \(x_3 = 7{,}8548\) and \(x_4 = 10{,}9955\).

Proof

We must show that the end conditions give a system of two equations with a nonzero solution exactly for equation (13.55), and that lemma 13.48 captures all the roots of this equation. The equation is the upper graph of figure 13.83, its roots the blackwhite dots.

  1. By theorem 13.40 and lemma 13.44, \(\varphi = C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x + C_3\operatorname{cosh}\beta x + C_4\operatorname{sinh}\beta x\). The clamp at \(x = 0\) (the wall, the curve leaves it horizontally): \(\varphi(0) = C_1 + C_3 = 0\) and \(\varphi'(0) = \beta(C_2 + C_4) = 0\), so \(C_3 = -C_1\), \(C_4 = -C_2\) and \(\varphi = C_1(\cos\beta x - \operatorname{cosh}\beta x) + C_2(\sin\beta x - \operatorname{sinh}\beta x)\).
  2. The derivatives are \(\varphi'' = -\beta^2\big[C_1(\cos\beta x + \operatorname{cosh}\beta x) + C_2(\sin\beta x + \operatorname{sinh}\beta x)\big]\) and \(\varphi''' = \beta^3\big[C_1(\sin\beta x - \operatorname{sinh}\beta x) - C_2(\cos\beta x + \operatorname{cosh}\beta x)\big]\) (theorem 8.13, lemma 9.47).
  3. The free end (the right end of figure 13.74), \(\varphi''(L) = \varphi'''(L) = 0\), gives with \(c = \cos x\), \(s = \sin x\), \(\mathrm{ch} = \operatorname{cosh}x\), \(\mathrm{sh} = \operatorname{sinh}x\) at \(x = \beta L\) the system
    \[(c + \mathrm{ch})\,C_1 + (s + \mathrm{sh})\,C_2 = 0 , \qquad (s - \mathrm{sh})\,C_1 - (c + \mathrm{ch})\,C_2 = 0 .\]
    This is the system of lemma 13.45 with \(A_{11} = c + \mathrm{ch}\), \(A_{12} = s + \mathrm{sh}\), \(A_{21} = s - \mathrm{sh}\), \(A_{22} = -(c + \mathrm{ch})\). The condition \((A_{11}, A_{12}) \ne (0, 0)\) holds for every \(x > 0\): for \(x \le \pi/2\), \(c \ge 0\) and \(\mathrm{ch} > 1\), so \(A_{11} > 0\), and for \(x > \pi/2\), \(\mathrm{sh} \ge \operatorname{sinh}(\pi/2) = 2{,}3013 > 1 \ge |s|\), so \(A_{12} > 0\).
  4. The determinant is \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21} = -(c + \mathrm{ch})^2 - (s + \mathrm{sh})(s - \mathrm{sh}) = -\big(c^2 + 2c\,\mathrm{ch} + \mathrm{ch}^2 + s^2 - \mathrm{sh}^2\big) = -2\,(1 + c\,\mathrm{ch})\), because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) (lemma 8.11) and \(\mathrm{ch}^2 - \mathrm{sh}^2 = \tfrac14\big((\mathrm{e}^x + \mathrm{e}^{-x})^2 - (\mathrm{e}^x - \mathrm{e}^{-x})^2\big) = 1\). By lemma 13.45 a nonzero solution exists if and only if equation (13.55) holds.
  5. Positive solutions of equation (13.55): because \(\mathrm{ch} > 0\) we need \(\cos x < 0\), which holds only on the parts of the blue curve below the axis, so \(x\) lies in the interval \(\big((2m - 1)\pi - \pi/2,\ (2m - 1)\pi + \pi/2\big)\) for some \(m \ge 1\) (lemma 8.11, items 3 and 4). We write \(x = n\pi + y\) with \(n = 2m - 1\) and \(|y| < \pi/2\). By corollary 8.16, \(\cos x = \cos n\pi\cos y - \sin n\pi\sin y = -\cos y\), and equation (13.55) becomes \(\cos y = \operatorname{sech}(n\pi + y)\). By lemma 13.48 it has exactly two solutions in each such interval. The intervals follow one another by size, so \(x_{2\mathrm{m}-1}\) is the left and \(x_{2\mathrm{m}}\) the right solution of the \(m\)-th interval, the first and the second blackwhite dot near a zero of the cosine.
  6. At a solution \(x_{\mathrm{r}} > \pi/2\), so \(A_{12} = s + \mathrm{sh} > 0\) (step 3). By lemma 13.45, \((C_1, C_2)\) is a multiple of the pair \((s + \mathrm{sh},\ -(c + \mathrm{ch}))\). Substituting into step 1 and dividing by \(-(s + \mathrm{sh})\) gives \(\varphi \propto \operatorname{cosh}\beta x - \cos\beta x - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}(\operatorname{sinh}\beta x - \sin\beta x)\), which is equation (13.56), the blue curve of the mode. From \(\beta^4 = \rho A\,\omega^2/EI\), \(\omega = \beta^2\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)} = x_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\omega_0\). Modes with \(\omega^2 \le 0\) do not exist by lemma 13.41.
  7. Numerical values (the blackwhite dots of the upper graph): the function \(f(x) = \cos x\operatorname{cosh}x + 1\) changes sign on short intervals: \(f(1{,}8751) > 0 > f(1{,}8752)\), \(f(4{,}6940) < 0 < f(4{,}6941)\), \(f(7{,}8547) > 0 > f(7{,}8548)\) and \(f(10{,}9955) < 0 < f(10{,}9956)\) (mpmath). By theorem 2.79 each of these intervals contains a root, and by step 5 it is the only root in its half of the interval \((\pi/2, 3\pi/2)\) or \((5\pi/2, 7\pi/2)\).

Source: CK example 13.3, PDF pp. 413 to 415: the frequency equation (6) and the values (7) on p. 414 (\(\lambda_1 L = 1{,}8751\), \(\lambda_2 L = 4{,}6941\), \(\lambda_3 L = 7{,}8548\), \(\lambda_4 L = 10{,}996\)), the shape (14) on p. 415. GR (E4.5.c), PDF p. 287, and table 4.3, PDF p. 289 (\(1{,}875\), \(4{,}694\), \(7{,}855\)). The existence and the number of roots by the intermediate value theorem are not from the source.

The shape of the first three modes is in figure 13.87, normalized so that the tip is \(1\) in each. The hatching on the left is the wall in which the cantilever is clamped. The grey dashed line is the undeformed axis of the beam. The blue curve is the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(x)\) of mode \(r\), whose number is written in the label beside it. The vertical gauge at the free end shows that the tip is normalized to \(1\). The blackwhite dots are nodes, points of the axis that stay at rest during the vibration. The arrow \(x\) shows the direction of the axis. The number of nodes (zeros of \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) inside the beam) is \(r - 1\) for these three modes: the first mode has none, the second mode has a node at \(0{,}7834\,L\), the third has two, at \(0{,}5035\,L\) and \(0{,}8677\,L\). This is a result of computation for the first three modes, we do not prove a general statement here.

Example 13.53 Frequencies of the 20 × 40 mm cantilever (frekvence konzole 20 × 40 mm)

The cantilever of the introduction: \(L = 1\) m, \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m², \(\rho A = 6{,}24\) kg/m, \(\omega_0 = 57{,}883\) 1/s. The coefficients are the orange ticks of figure 13.94. By theorem 13.52 the coefficients \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}/\omega_0 = x_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) are \(3{,}51602\), \(22{,}03449\), \(61{,}69721\) and \(120{,}9019\), and the frequencies \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}/(2\pi)\) are \(32{,}39\), \(202{,}99\), \(568{,}38\) and \(1113{,}79\) Hz (the spacing of the orange ticks on the line). The second is \(6{,}27\) times and the third \(17{,}5\) times the first. For the bar with a free end the ratio is \(1 : 3 : 5\), here it is about \(1 : 6{,}3 : 17{,}5\). The reason is that \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is proportional to \(x_{\mathrm{r}}^2\). At higher modes \(x_{\mathrm{r}}\) is close to \((2r - 1)\pi/2\), so there \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is approximately proportional to \((2r - 1)^2\) and not to \((2r - 1)\) as for the bar: \(\omega_3/\omega_2 = 2{,}800\) against \(25/9 = 2{,}778\). The first mode is the exception, because \(x_1 = 1{,}8751\) lies \(19\) % above \(\pi/2\) (the difference \(\delta_1 = 0{,}304\) below), so the ratio is \(1 : 6{,}3 : 17{,}5\) and not \(1 : 9 : 25\).

The difference from the nearest zero of the cosine disappears quickly: at higher roots the blackwhite dots lie almost on the zeros of the blue curve. From the equation \(\cos x_{\mathrm{r}} = -\operatorname{sech}x_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{r}} = (2r - 1)\pi/2 + \delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) it follows that \(|\sin\delta_{\mathrm{r}}| = \operatorname{sech}x_{\mathrm{r}}\), which gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = +0{,}304\), \(-0{,}0183\), \(+7{,}8 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(-3{,}4 \cdot 10^{-5}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, 4\). From the second step on, the difference is each time about \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi} = 0{,}043\) times smaller, because \(\operatorname{sech}x \approx 2\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{r}}\) grows by \(\pi\). So CK's \(x_4 = 10{,}996\) already equals \(7\pi/2 = 10{,}9956\) to three decimals.

Why is the differential equation alone not enough? Figure 13.88 shows the hatched wall on the left and the blue sine \(\varphi(x) = \sin(\pi x/L)\) with the undeformed axis and the free end on the right. The clamp requires the curve to leave the wall horizontally (grey line), but the sine has an orange tangent with a slope. Take the same function with \(L = 1\) m, a mode of the simply supported beam with \(\beta = \pi/L\). It solves the equation \(\varphi'''' = \beta^4\varphi\) and satisfies two of the four conditions of the cantilever, \(\varphi(0) = 0\) and \(\varphi''(L) = 0\). It does not satisfy the other two. The slope at the clamp is \(\varphi'(0) = \pi/L = 3{,}1416\) 1/m and not zero, the shear force at the free end is proportional to \(\varphi'''(L) = -(\pi/L)^3\cos\pi = +31{,}006\) 1/m³ and not zero. The frequency equation shows the same: at \(x = \beta L = \pi\) we have \(\cos\pi\,\cosh\pi + 1 = -10{,}592\), at \(x_1 = 1{,}8751\) it is \(+1{,}7 \cdot 10^{-5}\), which is zero up to the rounding of \(x_1\) to four decimals. The equation alone also accepts the sine, and a function becomes a mode of the cantilever only when it satisfies all four end conditions at once. These conditions select \(\beta L\) and the ratio \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\).

13.6.7 Cantilever with a tip mass

We fix a weight to the free end of a cantilever: a hammer has its head at the end of the handle, an acceleration sensor sits at the end of a measured beam. How does the weight change the frequencies? We expect it to lower them (the blue curve falls with the mass), since the same stiffness now has to move more mass. The computation tells by how much and shows two limits: without the weight we get the cantilever of theorem 13.52 (curve at mass zero), and with a very heavy weight the oscillator with one degree of freedom of section 9.1 (orange dashed curve), in which the beam is only a spring.

The left drawing of figure 13.89 shows the model. A beam of length \(L\) is clamped in the wall on the left, the grey dashed line is its axis at rest and the blue curve the deflection in the first mode. At the end is the point mass \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\), which moves with the displacement of the end \(w(L, t)\). The beam accelerates it, and it acts back on the end with the force \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) against the acceleration (end with a mass, theorem 13.43). The right drawing is the outcome: on the axes of the mass \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the first frequency \(f_1\), the blue curve is the exact first frequency of the beam of the introduction, and the orange dashed curve the frequency of the oscillator with one degree of freedom, which neglects the mass of the beam.

Figure 13.90 shows what the theorem proves. The curves are the left side of the equation for four weights. All start at \(2\) and fall. Above the horizontal axis the left side is positive, below it negative, and the crossing of the axis is the first frequency. A heavier weight moves the crossing nearer to zero.

Theorem 13.54 Modes of a cantilever with a tip mass (načini konzole z maso na koncu)

Let a uniform beam be clamped at \(x = 0\) (the wall) and carry at \(x = L\) a point mass \(m_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) without moment of inertia (definition 13.42, \(J_0 = 0\)). Let \(\mu_{\mathrm{k}} = m_{\mathrm{k}}/(\rho A L)\) be the ratio of the mass of the weight to the mass of the beam and \(h(x) = \sin x\operatorname{cosh}x - \cos x\operatorname{sinh}x\) as in lemma 13.49. A pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) with \(\omega > 0\) is a mode if and only if \(x = \beta L\) is a positive solution of the equation

\[1 + \cos x\,\operatorname{cosh}x - \mu_{\mathrm{k}}\,x\,h(x) = 0 \tag{13.57}\]

and \(\varphi\) is a nonzero multiple of the function (13.56) with the value of \(\sigma\) at this solution. The frequency is \(\omega = x^2\,\omega_0\). On \((0, \pi]\) the equation has exactly one solution \(x_1\), and it is smaller than the first root of the cantilever, \(x_1 < 1{,}8752\).

Proof

We must show that the end conditions give a system of two equations whose determinant is proportional to the left side of equation (13.57), and that this left side is strictly decreasing on \((0, \pi]\) from a positive to a negative value (curves of the figure).

  1. The clamp at \(x = 0\) gives, as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 13.52, \(\varphi = C_1(\cos\beta x - \operatorname{cosh}\beta x) + C_2(\sin\beta x - \operatorname{sinh}\beta x)\) (the curve leaves the wall horizontally).
  2. The end with the mass (the mass and its force): by theorem 13.43, \(EI\,\varphi''(L) = 0\) and \(EI\,\varphi'''(L) = -m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\omega^2\varphi(L)\). There is no moment because \(J_0 = 0\). The force is proportional to the displacement of the end, since the acceleration is \(-\omega^2\) times the displacement.
  3. From \(\beta^4 = \rho A\,\omega^2/EI\) (theorem 13.40) we get \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\omega^2/(EI\,\beta^3) = m_{\mathrm{k}}\,\beta/(\rho A) = \mu_{\mathrm{k}}\,\beta L\). With \(c\), \(s\), \(\mathrm{ch}\), \(\mathrm{sh}\) at \(x = \beta L\) the conditions read
    \[\begin{aligned} (c + \mathrm{ch})\,C_1 + (s + \mathrm{sh})\,C_2 &= 0 , \\ \big(s - \mathrm{sh} + \mu_{\mathrm{k}} x\,(c - \mathrm{ch})\big)\,C_1 + \big({-(c + \mathrm{ch})} + \mu_{\mathrm{k}} x\,(s - \mathrm{sh})\big)\,C_2 &= 0 . \end{aligned}\]
    The first row is the same as for the cantilever, the second has the added terms with \(\mu_{\mathrm{k}} x\).
  4. Determinant: the part without \(\mu_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(-2\,(1 + c\,\mathrm{ch})\) as in step 4 of the proof of theorem 13.52. The part with \(\mu_{\mathrm{k}} x\) is \((c + \mathrm{ch})(s - \mathrm{sh}) - (s + \mathrm{sh})(c - \mathrm{ch}) = 2\,(s\,\mathrm{ch} - c\,\mathrm{sh}) = 2\,h(x)\). Together \(-2\,\big(1 + c\,\mathrm{ch} - \mu_{\mathrm{k}} x\,h(x)\big)\), that is \(-2F(x)\), which is zero at the crossing of the curve with the axis. Because \(A_{12} = s + \mathrm{sh} > 0\) for every \(x > 0\) (for \(x \le \pi\) we have \(s \ge 0\) and \(\mathrm{sh} > 0\), for \(x > \pi\) we have \(\mathrm{sh} > 1\)), lemma 13.45 gives a nonzero solution exactly for equation (13.57), namely a multiple of the pair \((s + \mathrm{sh},\ -(c + \mathrm{ch}))\), which is the shape (13.56).
  5. Let \(F(x) = 1 + \cos x\operatorname{cosh}x - \mu_{\mathrm{k}}\,x\,h(x)\). The derivative of the first part is \(-\sin x\operatorname{cosh}x + \cos x\operatorname{sinh}x = -h(x)\), the derivative of \(h\) is \(2\sin x\operatorname{sinh}x\) (lemma 13.49, step 1), so \(F'(x) = -(1 + \mu_{\mathrm{k}})\,h(x) - 2\mu_{\mathrm{k}}\,x\sin x\operatorname{sinh}x\). On \((0, \pi)\) we have \(h > 0\) (the same lemma) and \(\sin x\operatorname{sinh}x > 0\), so \(F' < 0\) and \(F\) is strictly decreasing (theorem 1.85), like all four curves of the figure.
  6. Values: \(F(0) = 2 > 0\). At the first root of the cantilever \(x_1^{0} = 1{,}8751\) we have \(1 + \cos x\operatorname{cosh}x = 0\) up to rounding and \(-\mu_{\mathrm{k}}\,x\,h(x) < 0\), more precisely \(F(1{,}8752) < 0\), because there the first part is already negative (theorem 13.52, step 7). By theorem 2.79 \(F\) has a zero in \((0,\ 1{,}8752)\), by step 5 the only one on \((0, \pi]\). This is the move down along the blue curve: a larger mass, a lower frequency.
  7.
